desc:
There are n people numbered 0 to n - 1, each starting in a group of their own. You receive a list of operations ops, each of the form [type, a, b]:

  • type = 1: merge the group containing a with the group containing b (nothing happens if they are already the same group).
  • type = 2: report the current size of the group containing a. For this type b is always 0 and must be ignored.
  • type = 3: report 1 if a and b are currently in the same group, otherwise 0.

Return the reported values of all type 2 and type 3 operations, in the order the operations appear.

n = 6
ops = [[1,0,1],[1,2,3],[3,0,2],[1,1,3],[3,0,2],[2,3,0],[2,5,0]]

result = [0,1,4,1]

After the first two merges the groups are {0,1}, {2,3}, {4}, {5}, so person 0 and 2 are apart. After the third merge {0,1,2,3} is one group of size 4.
constraints: At least one operation has type 2 or 3
hints: Keeping a group label per person makes a merge cost O(n) in the worst case. What structure merges sets cheaply?
A disjoint-set (union-find) structure supports 'which group is this person in' (find) and 'merge two groups' (union).
Store the size at each root: when two roots are united add the smaller size into the larger root, and a size query is just size[find(a)]. A same-group query compares two roots.
editorial: This is a direct use of union-find with union by size. Every person starts as the root of its own set with size 1. A merge finds both roots, and if they differ, attaches the smaller tree below the larger one and adds the sizes. A size query returns the size stored at the root of a, and a same-group query checks whether the two roots are equal.

Union by size keeps the trees shallow, and path compression flattens them further, so each operation is O(α(n)), which is effectively constant. The whole sequence runs in about O((n + q) · α(n)) for q operations. Only the root's size entry is meaningful, so never read the size of a non-root node.
